headline: Parliament narrowly passes budget after all-night session
teaser: After fourteen hours of debate, lawmakers approved next year's budget by just three votes. The opposition calls the spending plan a gamble on growth that may never come.
text:
After fourteen hours of debate, lawmakers approved next year's budget by just three votes shortly before dawn on Monday.
The plan raises spending on infrastructure and schools while cutting subsidies for several industries. Supporters argue the investments will pay for themselves within a decade.
The opposition sharply criticised the outcome. Its finance spokesperson called the budget "a gamble on growth that may never come" and announced a constitutional review of two provisions.
The upper chamber is expected to vote on the package next week. Analysts expect it to pass there with a more comfortable majority.

headline: Cities turn to office conversions as rents keep climbing
teaser: Empty office towers could provide tens of thousands of new apartments. But converting them is slower and more expensive than many mayors had hoped.
text:
Empty office towers could provide tens of thousands of new apartments, according to a new study by a group of urban planning institutes.
Several cities have already launched pilot projects. In most cases, however, conversions take years and cost more per square metre than new construction.
Architects point to deep floor plans, a lack of windows and outdated plumbing as the main obstacles. "Not every building is suitable," one planner said. "But the ones that are should be converted quickly."
Tenant associations welcome the initiative but warn that converted flats must remain affordable.

headline: Shipping rates surge as key canal faces record low water
teaser: Freight costs for containers between Asia and Europe have doubled within a month. Retailers fear empty shelves before the holidays.
text:
Freight costs for containers between Asia and Europe have doubled within a month, as a prolonged drought forces authorities to limit traffic through one of the world's busiest canals.
Shipping companies are rerouting vessels around the continent, adding up to two weeks to journeys.
Retail associations warn that some goods may be in short supply before the holiday season. Economists expect the effect on inflation to be modest but noticeable.

headline: Freight operators warn of delays ahead of holiday season
teaser: Construction works and a shortage of drivers are slowing down goods trains across the country.
text:
Construction works on several main lines and a shortage of train drivers are slowing down goods trains across the country.
Operators say average delays have risen by a third compared with last year. Industry groups are calling on the government to prioritise freight on congested routes.
The rail infrastructure company said most construction sites would close by mid-December.

headline: Inside the race to build Europe's next chip factory
teaser: Billions in subsidies, a shortage of engineers and a tight deadline: a visit to the construction site.
text:
Billions in subsidies, a shortage of engineers and a tight deadline: the construction site on the edge of the city is one of the most closely watched industrial projects on the continent.
The plant is meant to produce chips for cars and industrial machines from 2029 onwards. More than two thousand workers are currently on site.
The biggest challenge is not the building itself but finding qualified staff. The company has started training programmes with three regional universities.
Critics question whether the public money would be better spent elsewhere.

headline: Solar output hits new record on sunniest day of the year
teaser: For several hours on Saturday, solar panels covered more than two thirds of the country's electricity demand. Grid operators say storage is now the bottleneck.
text:
For several hours on Saturday, solar panels covered more than two thirds of the country's electricity demand, according to figures from the national grid operators.
The record shows how quickly capacity has grown. It also highlights a problem: around midday, prices briefly turned negative because there was more power than could be used or stored.
Researchers say large batteries and flexible demand, for example from electric cars and heat pumps, will be key to making better use of solar power.

headline: Video consultations are here to stay, survey finds
teaser: Two in five patients have seen a doctor online in the past year. Most say they would do it again.
text:
Two in five patients have seen a doctor online in the past year, according to a survey by a health insurers' association.
Most respondents said they would use video consultations again, especially for follow-up appointments and prescriptions.
Doctors' associations are more cautious. They stress that online appointments cannot replace physical examinations.

headline: Teenage sprinter breaks national junior record
teaser: The 17-year-old ran the 100 metres in 10.08 seconds at the indoor season opener, beating a record that had stood for 31 years.
text:
The 17-year-old ran the 100 metres in 10.08 seconds at the season opener on Friday evening, beating a junior record that had stood for 31 years.
"I didn't look at the clock until I heard the crowd," the sprinter said after the race.
Coaches already see a candidate for the next Olympic relay team. The athletics federation said it would review its support programme for young talent.

headline: What the new tax rules mean for freelancers
teaser: Higher allowances, new deadlines and fewer forms: an overview of the most important changes.
text:
From January, freelancers will benefit from higher allowances and fewer forms, while some deadlines are moving forward.
Tax advisers recommend checking advance payments now, as the new rules may lower the amount due.
The finance ministry has published a calculator on its website to help self-employed people estimate the effect.

headline: Local newspapers find new readers with pay-what-you-want model
teaser: Instead of a paywall, a group of regional papers asks readers to decide what journalism is worth to them. The first results are surprising.
text:
Instead of a paywall, a group of regional newspapers asks readers to decide for themselves what local journalism is worth to them.
After one year, the number of paying readers has grown by almost a quarter. Most choose an amount close to the price of a regular subscription.
Media researchers say the model works best where readers feel a strong connection to their region.
